pubs.acs.org/synthbio Research Article # An Aldolase-Based New Pathway for Bioconversion of Formaldehyde and Ethanol into 1,3-Propanediol in Escherichia coli Hao Meng, Chuang Wang, Qipeng Yuan, Jie Ren,\* and An-Ping Zeng\* ![](images/98981b7415b19305d868c778a37a1046322a66605217bb1acdedff903e11996a.jpg) Cite This: ACS Synth. Biol. 2021, 10, 799−809 Read Online ## ACCESS Metrics & More ABSTRACT: Formaldehyde (HCHO) is a reactive one-carbon compound that is interesting for biosynthesis. The assimilation of HCHO depends on the catalysis of aldolase. Here, we present a novel synthetic pathway in E. coli to convert HCHO and ethanol into 1,3-propanediol (PDO) using a deoxyribose-5-phosphate aldolase (DERA). DERA condenses HCHO and acetaldehyde to form 3-hydroxypropionaldehyde, the direct precursor of PDO formation. This new pathway opens up the possibility to synthesize Article Recommendations \*sı Supporting Information ![](images/1a7b1c3511512261f51d199f049c5b8658128b0630582b019268800025203dc0.jpg) an appealing C3 compound from a C1 compound and a C2 compound without carbon loss in contrast to all the other known PDO synthetic pathways where typically 30−50% of the carbons are lost as $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and other byproducts. The pathway is successfully demonstrated by elaborating three metabolic modules. First, DERA from Thermotoga maritima was found to be eficient for the aldol condensation and PDO production module. For the module of acetaldehyde supply from ethanol, an alcohol dehydrogenase from Hansenula polymorpha was selected. For the HCHO supply module, the control of HCHO concentration and its utilization were shown to be important for achieving the assimilation of HCHO in recombinant E. coli cells. By deleting the gene frmA for endogenous conversion of HCHO to formate and controlling HCHO at a level of about 0.6 mM, the concentration and yield of PDO were increased from initially 5.67 mM (0.43 g/L) and 0.057 mol/mol to 17.35 mM (1.32 g/L) and 0.096 mol/mol in bioconversion of ethanol and HCHO with resting E. coli cells. Further engineering of DERA and the HCHO supply module is necessary to realize the potential of this promising metabolic pathway. KEYWORDS: one-carbon metabolism, formaldehyde, ethanol, deoxyribose-5-phosphate aldolase, 1,3-propanediol F ormaldehyde (HCHO) receives increasing interest as a reactive intermediate in the use of one-carbon (C1) compounds for biosynthesis. It can be converted from promising C1 feedstocks for sustainable bioproduction such as methane, methanol, and formate or generated from CO and biomass conversion.1−6 There are three major natural pathways for HCHO assimilation: the ribulose monophosphate (RuMP) pathway; the serine pathway; and the Calvin−Benson−Bassham (CBB) cycle.7−9 The RuMP pathway is regarded as the most eficient one in terms of ATP consumption and biomass yield. Recently, engineering of the RuMP pathway has attracted much attention to convert methanol for cell growth and value-added chemicals in heterotrophic organisms.10−12 I n the RuMP pathway, HCHO is reacted with ribulose 5- phosphate (Ru5P) to give arabino-3-hexulose-6-phosphate (Hu6P) under the catalysis of 3-hexulose-6-phosphate synthase (HPS); the latter is further isomerized to fructose 6-phosphate (F6P) by the enzyme 6-phospho-3-hexuloisomerase (PHI), and then metabolized in the pentose phosphate cycle to regenerate Ru5P or in central metabolic pathways to provide biomass precursors. However, this pathway is limited by the eficiency of ribulose 5-phosphate (Ru5P) regeneration.6 Wang at al. (2019)16 reported to use pyruvate as a HCHO acceptor catalyzed by 2-keto-4-hydroxybutyrate aldolase (KHB);13−16 they further developed this reaction into a new 1,3-propanediol (PDO) biosynthesis pathway.16 PDO is an important chemical compound with many applications in polymer, cosmetic, food, and pharmaceutical industries.17−20 The commercially utilized biosynthetic pathways to produce PDO are all based on glycerol either as the direct substrate in natural microorganisms or as an intermediate of glucose bioconversion in recombinant microbes (Figure 1). The latter typically needs to add vitamin ${ \bf B } _ { 1 2 }$ into the culture medium.21 Recently, several glycerol and thus vitamin ${ \bf B } _ { 1 2 }$ independent pathways for PDO biosynthesis have been proposed.16,19,22,23 One of the pathways is via homoserine and its further conversion to 4-hydroxy-2-ketobutyrate. After decarboxylation and reduction, 4-hydroxy-2-ketobutyrate is converted to PDO. Another pathway relies on a two-stepreduction based metabolic platform producing C3−C5 diols from amino acids.23 These pathways do not utilize expensive vitamin ${ \bf B } _ { 1 2 }$ as a cofactor, but both of them need to pay a large amount of NADPH and ATP. ![](images/5e38010539434ae7615ec7d6ca4c899ca75b0096524cac2a0551ad43350d45c2.jpg) ![](images/34a4680f531196ffa7f2e9b89ee2116a5e7bde7dc2930cdfd3841300aeec159b.jpg) Figure 1. Aldolases are powerful in synthetic biology because they can form new C−C bonds between a variety of aldehydes and ketones. They are widely used in the synthesis of long chain and complex carbon skeleton compounds. Wang et al. $( 2 0 1 9 ) ^ { 1 6 }$ obtained 4-hydroxy-2-ketobutyrate by an aldol condensation of pyruvate and HCHO. Methanol was used as a cosubstrate to supply NADH and to avoid ATP consumption in carboxylic reduction. Herein, we find not only pyruvate, but also acetaldehyde (ACALD) can be used as a new aldol acceptor for HCHO assimilation catalyzed by deoxyribose-5-phosphate aldolase (DERA, EC 4.1.2.4). 3-Hydroxypropionaldehyde (3-HPA) is formed via the aldol condensation of HCHO and ACALD, which can further convert into PDO. On the basis of this, a new and vitamin ${ \bf B } _ { 1 2 }$ independent PDO biosynthesis pathway is constructed, which is composed of three major enzymatic reactions: first, the oxidation of ethanol to ACALD; second, the aldol condensation ofHCHO and ACALD to $3 { \mathrm { - H P A } } ;$ and third, the reduction of 3-HPA to PDO. Compared to other major PDO synthetic pathways in which typically 30−50% of the carbons in the substrates are lost as CO and other byproducts, the new pathway has theoretically a 100% utilization of the carbons in the substrates (Figure 1).16,19−21,23−26 ## ■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Principle and Pathway Design of an Aldolase-Based New PDO Biosynthesis Route. In the previous work, aldolase was used to utilize HCHO and pyruvate for PDO production. 16 We noticed that the carboxyl group of pyruvate is not directly involved in the aldol condensation and is actually removed at the next step. It indicated that acetaldehyde (ACALD) is the real HCHO receptor in the C−C bond formation reaction (Figure 2). Therefore, we asked the question whether there is an aldolase that can catalyze the aldol condensation ofHCHO and ACALD, forming thereby 3-HPA, which can then be used for PDO production. Chemical aldol condensation of HCHO and ACALD was reported in literature.27,28 However, the reaction temperature was very high (above 250 °C), which can lead to serious side reactions such as dehydration, oligomerization, and polymerization. Biocatalysis can principally take place at environmental temperature and with high selectivity, and therefore overcomes these problems. A key issue here is to find a proper enzyme and integrate it into the metabolic pathway for PDO synthesis. Our systematic approach to engineer E. coli for PDO production using C1 compounds is based on a modular strain design of first an ACALD supply module using ethanol to provide ACALD and NADH, second a HCHO supply module, and finally a DERA-based PDO production module to convert ACALD and HCHO to PDO (Figure 3). For the implementation of this pathway, we first developed the last module (aldol condensation), which is the key part of the proposed pathway. Establishment of an Aldolase-Based PDO Production Module. To construct an aldolase-based PDO production module, diferent kinds of aldolases as listed in Table 116,29−31 were first screened for HCHO and ACALD condensation. They were coexpressed with DhaT from K. pneumoniae32 in E. coli BL21(DE3) for PDO synthesis. An acetaldehyde-dependent deoxyribose-5-phosphate aldolase from E. coli K-12 (DERA ) turned out to well catalyze the condensation of HCHO and $\mathrm { A C A L D . } ^ { 3 3 } 1 . 0 2 \pm 0 . 0 3$ mM $( 7 7 . 6 \pm 2 . 2 8 ~ \mathrm { m g / L } )$ PDO were formed in a preliminary trial with 10 mM of HCHO and ACALD added after 2 h. To prove that the added HCHO and ACALD were condensed into the synthesis of PDO, we used 13C-HCHO or 13C-ACALD as cosubstrate for carrying out the biosynthesis. As shown in Figure 4 the ratio of the peaks around $m / z 1 6 2 . 1$ and $m / z \ : 1 6 3 . 1 $ are almost the same in the unlabeled standard sample and the 13C-labled samples. It confirmed that the synthesis of PDO totally depends on HCHO and ACALD added. ![](images/2c2f2bdd1289f6c93f5832cd7a5360e788073f0382407f9d6a58e81693577bce.jpg) Figure 3. DERA-based C1 new metabolic pathway for PDO production proposed in this work, which is divided into three modules for its implementation: ACALD supply module, HCHO supply module, and DERA-based PDO production module. In order to select a more eficient DERA for PDO production, we tested four kinds ofDERAs from heat-resistant bacteria since it was suggested that heat resistance is related to aldehyde tolerance.34 We examined them by coexpressing them individually with DhaT in E. coli BL21(DE3). The results are summarized in Table 2. The engineered strain with incorporation of $\mathrm { { D E R A } _ { \mathrm { { T M A } } } }$ from Thermotoga maritima gave the highest PDO concentration and yield from HCHO and ACALD, reaching $8 . 2 0 \pm 0 . 0 4$ mM and 0.082 mol/mol respectively after 12 h of bioconversion. But the $\mathrm { { D E R A } _ { \mathrm { { T M A } } } }$ -catalyzed condensation ofHCHO and ACALD is still the bottleneck ofthis module as shown by the results using purified $\mathrm { { D E R A } _ { \mathrm { { T M A } } } }$ and DhaT in demonstration of this module (Figure S1B). The results revealed that DhaT could support at least ten times of the activity of $\mathrm { { D E R A } _ { \mathrm { { T M A } } } }$ without accumulation of 3-HPA. DERAs can be used to catalyze the aldol condensation of HCHO and ACALD into 3-HPA, but their activity might be limited by their poor stability toward high aldehyde concentrations.35 Sakuraba et al. Considering both the specific activity and the tolerance toward HCHO, $\mathrm { { D E R A } _ { \mathrm { { T M A } } } }$ turned out to be the most promising one for aldol condensation of HCHO and ACALD. We therefore focused on this enzyme in further study. First, the $K _ { m }$ value of $\mathrm { { D E R A } _ { \mathrm { { T M A } } } }$ for HCHO was estimated by measuring more data under low HCHO concentrations $\left( 1 { - } 1 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \right)$ . The $K _ { m }$ value of $\mathbf { \Delta } _ { \mathrm { D E R A _ { T M A } } } ^ { \mathrm { ^ { * } m e a t } }$ for HCHO is higher than that of HPS for the condensation of HCHO and ribulose-5-phosphate, but lower (by nearly 200 times) than that of KHB for the condensation of HCHO and pyruvate (Table 3). A low $K _ { m }$ value for HCHO is desired for DERA-based metabolic engineering of cells to keep both a high eficiency of aldol condensation and an adequate cell growth. Implementation of an ACALD Supply Module for DERA-Based PDO Production. Having selected a promising DERA enzyme, several other issues should be addressed for developing an eficient DERA-based PDO production. First of all, a supply or production module of ACALD should be developed. A direct addition ofACALD would be too expensive or inconvenient for the operation and harmful for the biocatalyst. In such a case the balance of reducing power (NADH) is also a critical issue. To avoid the direct use of ACALD and at the same time to achieve a NADH balance, we proposed to generate ACALD from ethanol as outlined in Figures 1 and 2. For this purpose, a suitable alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) should be selected. Among the large number of ADHs, we chose the ADH from Hansenula polymorpha (HpADH1, EC 1.1.1.1) which showed good performance on converting ethanol to acetaldehyde.39,40 PDO production with this new module was demonstrated in vitro using purified proteins, showing that HpADH1 can provide enough ACALD for the PDO formation (Figures S1C,D). We used $^ { \mathrm { { \sc ~ \ y ~ } } _ { 1 3 } } \mathrm { { C } }$ -ethanol and HCHO as cosubstrates to verify the PDO production from such an ACALD supply module (Figure 6A). Using E. coli carrying $\mathrm { { D E R A } _ { T M A } }$ and DhaT, ethanol and HCHO were successfully converted to PDO in a whole-cell bioconversion (Figure 6B). The PDO formation was significantly improved from $5 . 6 7 \pm 0 . 2 5$ mM (0.43 g/L) and 0.057 mol/mol using a strain without HpADH1 expression to 10.91 ± 0.08 mM (0.83 g/L) and 0.11 mol/mol with HpADH1 expression (Figure 6C). Methanol as Substrate for HCHO. To develop a HCHO supply module, methanol was first used as substrate. We selected a methanol dehydrogenase (Mdh2, EC 1.1.1.244) to catalyze the oxidation of methanol to HCHO and expressed it in the BF17 strain. Whole-cell bioconversion using methanol and ethanol as cosubstrates was carried out with this strain. After 42 h, PDO reached only 1.05 mM with considerable amounts of other diols. This pathway was also demonstrated in vitro using purified proteins. The results showed that the activity of methanol dehydrogenase is the bottleneck (Figure S1E). Identification of Diol Byproducts. Nemr et al. (2018) showed that $\mathrm { { D E R A } _ { \mathrm { { T M A } } } }$ also has a high activity toward selfpolymerization of $\mathrm { A \bar { C } A L D . ^ { 3 6 , 4 2 } }$ We hypothesize that $\mathrm { { D E R A } _ { \mathrm { { T M A } } } }$ may also catalyze the condensation of ACALD with other aldehydes such as 3-HPA which is a key intermediate of the proposed PDO biosynthesis pathway. Indeed, several diols were formed in the bioconversion system using HCHO and ethanol as the substrates (Figure 7A). $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } .$ -ethanol was used as substrate to confirm the diol byproducts in batch bioconversion. As shown in Figure 7B−D, the GC-MS spectra ofsamples showed that the byproducts include 1,3-butanediol (1,3-BDO) (m/z 178.1), 3,5- dihydroxypentanal $\left( m / z 2 0 6 . 1 \right)$ , and 3,5-dihydroxyhexanal (m/ $z 2 \dot { 2 } 1 . 1 )$ . The possible synthetic routes of them are inferred as follows: two molecules of ACALD are condensed into 3- hydroxybutyraldehyde, which is further reduced to $^ { 1 , 3 \cdot }$ -BDO by DhaT; ACALD and 3-HPA are condensed to form $^ { 3 , 5 \mathrm { - } }$ dihydroxypentanal, a C5 diol aldehyde; ACALD and 3- hydroxybutyraldehyde were condensed to form $^ { 3 , 5 \cdot }$ -dihydroxyhexanal, a C6 diol aldehyde (Figure 7E). It seems that DhaT did not prefer the C6 and C5 aldehydes, since the corresponding alcohols were not found in the MS spectra. Interestingly, the diol byproducts were found to be generated only when HCHO was nearly completely consumed. We further examined the relationship ofHCHO concentration and diol byproducts production in vitro. It was found that a HCHO concentration above 0.6 mM can strongly inhibit the self-condensation of ACALD and its condensation with 3-HPA (Figure 7F). In the following bioconversion experiments the HCHO concentration was thus kept over 0.6 mM to eliminate the formation ofdiol byproducts. Eliminating Diol Byproducts and Increasing the Production in Fed-Batch Bioconversion. In order to increase the yield of PDO and eliminate the diol byproducts, we performed fed-batch bioconversion to maintain the amount ofHCHO above a certain level (Figure 8). In a 40 mL whole-cell bioconversion system, a total volume of 100 mM HCHO was added in ten times interval as shown in Figure 8. As expected, no diol byproducts were produced and the production ofPDO was increased to $1 7 . 3 5 \pm 0 . 5 8$ mM $\left( 1 . 3 2 \pm 0 . 0 4 \ : \mathrm { g / L } \right)$ with a yield of 0.096 mol/mol at 24 h compared to 12.75 mM and 0.128 mol/ mol in the batch bioconversion without significant accumulations of ACALD and 3-HPA (Figure 6D). Surprisingly, in addition to PDO, a major part of the HCHO was converted to methanol (56.47 mM at 30 h) and obviously some HCHO was converted to formate despite the knockout of the frmA gene. Concerning the generation of methanol, it is obviously because of expression of HpADH1 that speeds up the conversion of HCHO to methanol. There may be some unclear reasons for the massive consumption of HCHO at the beginning (1 h) because HpADH1 was not expressed well and the activity toward HCHO is not high (0.83 U in vitro). Three metabolic modules were elaborated: a DERA-based PDO production module, an ACALD supply module and a HCHO supply module. This new pathway opens up the possibility to synthesize an appealing C3 compound from a C1 and a C2 compound without carbon loss in theory. This work has enriched the application of C1 compounds by using ACALD as a new HCHO acceptor in biocatalysis. Compared the KHB-based pathway,16 DERA shows a higher afinity for HCHO than KHB. It should be mentioned that the afinity to HCHO and activity of the most appealing enzyme $\mathrm { { D E R A } _ { \mathrm { { T M A } } } }$ applied here are still quite limited. Protein engineering of this enzyme and systems metabolic engineering work for host strain should be very meaningful for the direct use of C1 compounds for value-added products production in synthetic biology. Furthermore, the maintenance ofa certain level ofintracellular HCHO is important to avoid the self-polymerization of ACALD and the formation of other diol byproducts. In this context, it is also worth mentioning that the three reactions of the proposed pathway are all reversible. Although the standard Gibbs free energy for the aldol condensation of HCHO and ACALD is estimated to be negative (about −3.702 kJ/mol) and the reaction is thus thermodynamically feasible, driving force or equilibrium of the pathway may represent a critical issue in further consideration.
